items.title: :Independent verification pass at 59ec3b4 — design notes, planted-defect results (7/11 caught), tests included
items.body:
### Kontext version

v1.2.0 (main @ 59ec3b4)

### OS and architecture

-

### Command

```
kontext hook --agent claude   (PreToolUse, tool_input.command = "rm  -rf /", policy forbids "rm -rf /")
```


### Expected behavior

A forbid on `rm -rf /` also matches obvious variants of the same command (extra whitespace,
quoting), or the docs state plainly that policies match raw input text.

### Actual behavior


`rm  -rf /` (two spaces) is allowed: policy evaluation runs on the raw `tool_input`, and the only
normalizer (`riskclassifier.NormalizeCommand`) feeds the advisory classifier, not the policy path.
Reproduction: `TestIA4_NoCanonicalizationLayer` in
https://github.com/blu400codes/trenyx-verify-002-kontext/tree/main/02-independent-tests.

---

Hi — I run a small verification practice and used this repo as a public sample of the method: an
AI-assisted Go codebase (121 of 279 commits Claude co-authored) guarding AI agents, with a serious
test suite. No relationship, nothing commissioned. Everything below is reproducible:
https://github.com/blu400codes/trenyx-verify-002-kontext (attack plan hashed and posted publicly
before I read a line; 27 blind tests; 11 planted defects run against your suite).

First, the headline is good: the decision core is fail-closed by construction and your tests caught
7 of 11 planted semantic defects — including every plant on the Cedar mapper, the breaker, policy
metadata validation, forbid-wins, and the observe-mode reason text. That's the strongest suite I've
put this method against. The four that escaped: an unknown hook-mode string defaulting to observe
(ParseMode's error branch has no test), the Cedar evaluator not refreshing when the deployment
identity changes, a silently lost deferred ledger record (no test asserts the failure is logged),
and a command truncated before policy evaluation (no long-command policy test).

Design notes, no security impact claimed:
- Policy matching runs on raw tool input; `rm  -rf /` (two spaces) is not matched by a forbid on
  `rm -rf /`. Inherent to Cedar-on-raw-input, but worth a prominent line for policy authors, or
  normalized context fields (argv-split, whitespace-collapsed).
- Deferred decision records are best-effort by design (answer first, write later, failures logged
  and counted, not retried); the README's "records the decision and outcome in an authorization
  ledger" reads stronger than that. One sentence would align them.
- Remote-posture outage handling fails closed only while the on-disk policy cache is readable and
  claims enforce; a missing cache fails open (documented). The guarded agent runs as the user who
  owns that file. The README correctly defers this to a sandbox — a sentence next to the enforce
  switch saying the sandbox is load-bearing would help operators.
- Under static enforce, an expired cache denies everything (enforcement_not_ready) — intended
  fail-closed, but the offline symptom and maxAge deserve a doc line.

Two enforcement-relevant items went through your private advisory channel per SECURITY.md rather
than here. Findings write-up publishes in the repo above after a fix or ~14 days; corrections
welcome — tell me what I got wrong.

### Relevant logs or screenshots

```shell
trenyx_cedareval_test.go:113: variant 'rm  -rf /' (double space) was ALLOWED: raw-input matching, no canonical form

Baseline: go test -count=1 ./...  → 37 packages ok, 0 failures (Go 1.25, commit 59ec3b4)
Planted-defect matrix: 7 / 11 caught — see 03-planted-defects/matrix.md in the linked repo
```

items.title: Add cryptographically signed audit receipts for authorization decisions
items.body:
Authorization decisions need to produce **tamper-evident receipts** — cryptographically signed records that capture the full context of each decision: what action was attempted, who initiated it, the session state, and what the system decided (and why). Each receipt is signed so it can be verified offline by a third party, and receipts are hash-chained together so that deletions and reorderings are detectable, not just modifications.

The point: the decision log becomes independently verifiable rather than something you just have to trust.

## Signing

Signing algorithm (any of):
- Ed25519
- ECDSA P-256
- RSA-2048 minimum

What gets signed: canonical serialization of the receipt contents — meaning deterministic, reproducible byte representation.

Public keys must be available for offline verification.

## Receipt contents

Each receipt must contain:

- **Action**: tool, operation, parameters, timestamp
- **Context**: session identifier, accumulated context at decision time
- **Identity**: human principal, service identity, agent identity, role/privilege scope
- **Decision**: result (ALLOW/DENY/MODIFY/STEP_UP/DEFER), matched policy, reason
- **Approval** (if applicable): approver identity, decision, timestamp
- **Deferral** (if applicable): deferral reason, resolution method, resolution timestamp
- **Outcome**: execution result, error details if failed
- **Signature**: cryptographic signature verifiable offline

items.title: Architecture: converge Guard and hosted runtimes behind one local runtime
items.body:
## Problem The CLI currently has two runtime architectures evolving in parallel: * `kontext guard start`: local Guard daemon, persistent Claude hooks, local risk policy, SQLite/dashboard. * `kontext start`: hosted/session sidecar, temporary Claude settings, Unix socket, hosted hook decisions, credential injection. These paths solve related problems but duplicate hook semantics, runtime boundaries, session behavior, policy evaluation, and storage/transport concerns. If we keep extending both independently, the eventual cutover to a unified local-first runtime becomes a large, risky rewrite. ## Target architecture direction Converge both paths behind one local runtime contract: ```text Claude PreToolUse/PostToolUse -> kontext hook --agent claude -> Unix socket -> LocalRuntimeService -> RuntimeCore -> policy / credentials / events / sync ``` There should be one shared runtime core with two ways to host it: * Local/dev: `kontext start` starts the runtime for a Claude session, launches Claude, and shuts the runtime down when Claude exits. * Managed/enterprise: `kontext daemon` keeps the same runtime running in the background. Claude can be launched normally, and managed Claude hook config calls `kontext hook --agent claude`, which talks to the daemon. Runtime logic should be shared. Only lifecycle, endpoint discovery, and session ownership should differ. ## Architecture decisions already made * Enforcement uses Claude command hooks, not Claude HTTP hooks. * Per-tool command hook process overhead is acceptable because fail-closed blocking is non-negotiable. * HTTP remains appropriate for dashboard/diagnostics/query APIs, not hook enforcement. * Hosted ConnectRPC remains a control-plane/provider integration, not the local enforcement architecture. * Policy and credential providers should be pluggable. * Hosted policy should be mirrorable locally for fast/offline evaluation. * Risk scoring should run locally near the agent and feed policy evaluation. * Persistence is for policy/model snapshots, event/audit state, rollback, and sync cursors. The enforcement hot path should use in-memory state. ## Proposed progression This should be implemented as a sequence of small, working steps rather than one large cutover. 1. kontext-security/kontext-cli#98
Normalize hook semantics across hosted and local runtimes. This creates the shared hook domain model and removes the worst duplication. 2. Introduce a shared hook evaluator interface
Existing hosted and Guard paths should both evaluate the same internal contract, for example `hook.Event -> hook.Result`, while keeping behavior unchanged. 3. Separate enforcement from telemetry
Make `PreToolUse -> EvaluateHook` and `PostToolUse/UserPromptSubmit -> IngestEvent` explicit in code and tests. 4. Introduce `RuntimeCore` as a facade
Add the target runtime seam while initially delegating to existing hosted/Guard implementations. 5. Move Guard policy behind a policy provider
Wrap the current Guard risk engine as a provider without rewriting it. 6. Move hosted hook decisions behind a policy provider
Wrap current hosted `ProcessHookEvent` behavior behind the same provider contract. 7. Add local policy/model persistence and mirroring
Add durable policy/model snapshots, activation/rollback metadata, and in-memory hot-path activation. 8. Introduce `LocalRuntimeService`
Expose the runtime through a local Unix-socket service boundary. Existing sidecar DTOs/protos should remain boundary types with thin conversions. 9. Unify the hook command path
Make `kontext hook --agent claude` the canonical command hook handler. Keep old Guard hook commands as compatibility aliases until cutover is complete. 10. Move `kontext start` onto the shared runtime
The dev/session path should start the same runtime core and expose the same local service boundary. 11. Move Guard daemon onto the shared runtime
The daemon/dashboard path should preserve dashboard HTTP but route hook decisions through `RuntimeCore`. 12. Unify session lifecycle
Add `OpenSession`, `CloseSession`, and daemon-side `EnsureSessionForEvent` semantics so wrapper-owned and daemon-observed sessions share one model. 13. Add credential provider abstraction
Move hosted token exchange and local/noop credential behavior behind provider interfaces after hook/runtime unification is stable. 14. Compatibility cleanup
Remove duplicate internal hook/runtime contracts and retire old command aliases once both modes use the shared core. ## Acceptance criteria for the architecture track * Existing hosted and Guard behavior remains covered by tests throughout the progression. * No step requires a full cutover of both runtimes at once. * Hook semantics are represented once internally. * Runtime policy/credential/session logic does not live in the hook process. * Sidecar and daemon use the same runtime core. * Hook enforcement remains fail-closed for protected `PreToolUse` operations. * `go test ./...` and `go vet ./...` pass at each major step. ## Out of scope * Rewriting Guard policy/risk logic in the first step. * Changing hosted backend policy semantics as part of normalization. * Adding Claude HTTP hook enforcement mode. * Removing compatibility aliases before both paths are on the shared runtime.

items.title: Normalize hook semantics across hosted and local runtimes
items.body:
## Problem

The CLI currently represents the same hook flow in several internal shapes:

- `agent.HookEvent`
- `hookruntime.Event`
- `sidecar.EvaluateRequest` / `EvaluateResult`
- `guard/risk.HookEvent`

These all describe the same thing: an agent hook event is evaluated and returns a decision.

Because the concept is redefined in multiple layers, hosted mode and local Guard each remap fields, decisions, and fallback behavior separately.

## Why this matters

This makes the hook runtime harder to extend safely.

Concrete risks:

- New agents need duplicate adapter/runtime plumbing.
- Hosted and local paths can preserve different hook fields.
- Decisions are translated between multiple formats.
- Sidecar transport DTOs and internal runtime semantics are mixed.
- Missing-sidecar behavior can fail open unless it is explicit and tested.

## Target

Introduce one internal hook domain model, likely `internal/hook`.

It should own:

- `Event`
- `Result`
- `Decision`
- `HookName`

`internal/hook` is the shared model only. It should not route to hosted or local evaluators.

Target flow:

```text
Agent adapter
  -> hook.Event
  -> hookruntime runner
  -> hosted sidecar evaluator OR local Guard evaluator
  -> hook.Result
  -> agent response
```

Hosted sidecar and local Guard should remain separate evaluator implementations, but both should evaluate the same internal contract:

```go
hook.Event -> hook.Result
```

Backend proto messages and sidecar socket request/response structs should stay as boundary DTOs with thin, tested conversion functions.

## Acceptance criteria

- One internal definition exists for hook names, decisions, and result semantics.
- Agent adapters decode external hook input into `hook.Event`.
- The hookruntime runner owns routing to hosted/local evaluators.
- Hosted mode evaluates `hook.Event -> hook.Result`.
- Local Guard evaluates `hook.Event -> hook.Result`.
- Sidecar request/response structs are clearly boundary DTOs.
- Backend proto types do not leak into evaluator logic.
- Missing `KONTEXT_SOCKET` behavior is explicit and covered by tests.
- Existing hosted and Guard behavior remains covered by tests.
- `go test ./...` and `go vet ./...` pass.

## Out of scope

- Rewriting the Guard risk engine.
- Changing backend policy semantics.
- Changing provider or credential behavior.
- Keeping duplicate internal hook contracts for compatibility.

items.title: Unify hook adapter runtime across Guard and hosted mode

labels.name: area:kontext
labels.description: Kontext CLI and model pipeline work

items.body:
## Problem

We are about to add Cursor hook support, but the CLI currently has two separate hook paths:

- Hosted mode: `kontext start --agent claude` generates hooks that call `kontext hook --agent claude`, then events go through `internal/agent` / `internal/hook` into the sidecar and hosted backend.
- Guard mode: `kontext guard start` installs hooks that call `kontext guard hook claude-code`, then events go through the Guard hook runtime into the local daemon and risk engine.

PR #90 refactors the Guard hook runtime, but that adapter boundary is still Guard-specific. If we add Cursor only there, we will solve local Guard while likely duplicating Cursor protocol handling later for hosted mode.

## Why this matters

Cursor support should not require two implementations of the same agent hook protocol. The agent-specific adapter should understand Claude or Cursor hook JSON once, then route the normalized action to whichever runtime is active.

## Proposed architecture

Create one shared hook adapter/runtime layer:

```text
agent hook protocol adapters
  Claude adapter
  Cursor adapter

shared normalized event/action model

runtimes / sinks
  hosted sink -> sidecar -> backend ProcessHookEvent
  guard sink  -> local daemon -> risk decision
```

Guard and hosted mode should share the same protocol adapters and normalized event model. They should differ only in the processor/sink:

- Guard processor: local daemon, local risk decision, local SQLite/dashboard.
- Hosted processor: sidecar, hosted `ProcessHookEvent`, governed session traces.

## Suggested scope

- Move the hook runtime out of `internal/guard` into a shared package.
- Replace Guard-specific `risk.HookEvent` at the runtime boundary with a neutral hook/action event type.
- Add a Guard policy/processor adapter that maps neutral events into the existing risk model.
- Merge or delete the older `internal/agent` / `internal/hook` abstraction so there is one hook runtime path.
- Keep install/config code agent-specific, because Claude settings and Cursor `.cursor/hooks.json` are different surfaces.

## Acceptance criteria

- Claude hook decoding/encoding is implemented once and works for both Guard and hosted mode.
- Cursor support can be added as one adapter and reused by both Guard and hosted mode.
- Guard and hosted mode choose different processors/sinks without duplicating agent protocol logic.
- The implementation follows the repo's hard-cutover approach: no long-term parallel compatibility layer.

items.title: Support Codex and Gemini agents with full governance parity
items.body:
cc @tumberger

## Goal

Extend `kontext start --agent <name>` to support OpenAI Codex CLI and Google Gemini CLI alongside Claude Code, with the same behavior: auth, credential injection from `.env.kontext`, hook telemetry streamed to the sidecar, and allow/deny decisions.

## Compatibility research

### Gemini CLI — full parity achievable
- Ships a mainline hook system with `BeforeTool`, `AfterTool`, `UserPromptSubmit`-equivalent events in `.gemini/settings.json` under a top-level `hooks` key.
- Same JSON-over-stdin contract as Claude, same `exit 2` / `{"decision":"deny"}` semantics. Our existing `HookEvent` maps 1:1 with minor event-name normalization.
- Hooks fire on every built-in tool and MCP tool (not shell-only).
- Docs: https://github.com/google-gemini/gemini-cli/tree/main/docs/hooks

### Codex CLI — near parity, one known gap
- Experimental hooks under `[hooks]` in `config.toml` with `experimental_hooks = true`. Stdin field names already match Claude (`hook_event_name`, `tool_name`, `tool_input`, `tool_response`, `cwd`, `session_id`).
- `PreToolUse` / `PostToolUse` fire for `shell` (incl. `local_shell`), `apply_patch`, and MCP tools (`mcp__<server>__<tool>`). Built-in `read_file` / `write_file` as distinct tools are NOT covered — edits go through `apply_patch` instead, which IS covered.
- `CODEX_HOME` env var cleanly redirects config dir for per-session isolation.

### Claude Code — unchanged, current implementation remains

## Proposed design

### Interface change (`internal/agent/agent.go`)

```go
type Agent interface {
    Name() string
    Binary() string
    Prepare(sessionDir, kontextBin string) (PrepareResult, error)
    DecodeHookInput([]byte) (*HookEvent, error)
    EncodeAllow(*HookEvent, string) ([]byte, error)
    EncodeDeny(*HookEvent, string) ([]byte, error)
}

type PrepareResult struct {
    Args       []string
    Env        []string
    WorkingDir string
}
```

Each adapter owns its own settings writer and launch argv/env. `HookEvent` itself is unchanged; adapters normalize native event names to internal `PreToolUse` / `PostToolUse` / `UserPromptSubmit`.

### Per-agent Prepare

- **Claude**: writes `<sessionDir>/settings.json`, returns `Args=["--settings", path]`. (Current behavior, moved behind the interface.)
- **Codex**: writes `<sessionDir>/.codex/config.toml` with `experimental_hooks = true` and `[hooks.pre_tool_use]` / `[hooks.post_tool_use]` / `[hooks.user_prompt_submit]` command entries pointing at `kontext hook --agent codex`. Returns `Env=["CODEX_HOME=<sessionDir>/.codex"]`.
- **Gemini**: writes a session-scoped `.gemini/settings.json` with a `hooks` object. See open question below for exact placement.

### Launcher refactor (`internal/run/run.go`)

Replace `launchAgentWithSettings` with `launchAgent(a agent.Agent, userArgs, userEnv []string)`. It calls `a.Prepare(...)`, prepends `PrepareResult.Args` to filtered user args, merges env, applies `WorkingDir`, then `exec.LookPath(a.Binary())`. `GenerateSettings` in `internal/run/hooks.go` moves into the Claude adapter.

### Flag filtering per agent

Each agent has different flags to strip from pass-through user args (Claude has `--settings`, `--bare`, `--dangerously-skip-permissions`; Codex and Gemini will have their own). Move `filterArgs` into the `Agent` interface or a per-agent method.

## Open question

Gemini has no `--settings <path>` flag and no `GEMINI_CONFIG_DIR` env var. Three options for injecting our hook config:

- **(a)** Write to `<CWD>/.gemini/settings.json` (workspace scope, highest precedence). Clean, but leaves a file in the user's repo that needs defer-based cleanup and a stale-file check on next start.
- **(b)** Set `GEMINI_CLI_SYSTEM_SETTINGS_PATH` to a per-session file. No filesystem mutation, but system scope is lowest precedence — user's own `hooks: {}` would silently override us.
- **(c)** Merge into `~/.gemini/settings.json` on start, restore on exit. Reliable but mutates user's global config; risky on crash.

Recommendation: **(a)** — workspace scoped with defer cleanup and stale-file recovery on next `kontext start`.

## Scope

- Ship Codex with hook-based governance; document the `apply_patch` vs distinct `write_file` nuance in the README.
- Ship Gemini with full hook parity.
- Update the supported-agents table in README.
- No sidecar / backend / credential-resolution changes required — existing infrastructure is agent-agnostic.

## Out of scope

- PTY/supervisor fallbacks for gaps (revisit if upstream agents regress).
- Cursor support (separate issue).

items.title: fix: sidecar retries dead refresh token indefinitely after invalid_grant
items.body:
## Problem

When the OIDC refresh token becomes invalid (expired or revoked), the sidecar's heartbeat loop retries the same dead refresh token every 30 seconds indefinitely. The stale session remains in the keychain, so the problem persists until the user manually runs `kontext login`.

**Observed logs:**
```
sidecar: heartbeat: unavailable: token refresh: token expired and refresh failed: refresh token: oauth2: "invalid_grant"
```

## Root Cause

`newSessionTokenSource` in `internal/run/run.go` has no recovery path when `RefreshSession` returns `invalid_grant`. The error is returned, but the stale session is never cleared — so the next heartbeat retries with the same dead token.

## Fix

1. Detect `invalid_grant` and stop retrying
2. Clear the stale session from keychain
3. Log a message telling the user to run `kontext login`

items.title: fix: sidecar heartbeat spams repeated errors without backoff
items.body:
## Problem

The sidecar heartbeat loop runs on a fixed 30s ticker and logs every failure with `log.Printf`:

```go
if err := s.client.Heartbeat(ctx, s.sessionID); err != nil {
    log.Printf("sidecar: heartbeat: %v", err)
}
```

When the network goes down (DNS failure, WiFi switch, laptop sleep/wake), this produces the same error message every 30 seconds for the rest of the session:

```
2026/04/09 10:41:17 sidecar: heartbeat: unavailable: token refresh: token expired and refresh failed: oauth discovery: discovery request: Get "https://api.kontext.security/.well-known/oauth-authorization-server": dial tcp: lookup api.kontext.security: no such host
2026/04/09 10:41:47 sidecar: heartbeat: unavailable: ...
2026/04/09 10:42:17 sidecar: heartbeat: unavailable: ...
```

Same issue applies to `ingestEvent` failures at line 122-124.

## Expected behavior

1. **Exponential backoff** on consecutive failures (30s → 60s → 120s → cap at 5min)
2. **Deduplicate logs** — print the error on first occurrence and when it changes, not every tick
3. **Log recovery** — print a success message when connectivity returns after a failure streak
4. **Reset backoff** on success — return to the normal 30s interval once a heartbeat succeeds

## Example output

```
sidecar: heartbeat failed: dial tcp: lookup api.kontext.security: no such host (retrying with backoff)
sidecar: heartbeat recovered after 3m20s
```

items.title: fix: store hook_event, tool_use_id, and tool_input as indexed columns instead of JSON blobs
items.body:
## Problem

Several high-value fields are buried inside `request_json` JSON blobs in the `mcp_events` table instead of being stored as first-class indexed columns:

| Field | Current storage | Impact |
|---|---|---|
| `hook_event` | Inside `request_json.hookEvent` | Cannot efficiently query "all PreToolUse events" without JSON path scan |
| `tool_use_id` | Inside `request_json.toolUseId` | Cannot efficiently correlate Pre/Post events without JSON extraction |
| `tool_input` | Inside `request_json.toolInput` | Cannot index or filter by input properties |

Meanwhile `tool_name` and `response_json` are already proper columns.

## Fix

This is an API/DB concern, not a CLI concern. The API handler should extract these fields from the proto message and store them in dedicated columns:

1. Add `hook_event` column to `mcp_events` (or use the existing `event_type` column more precisely)
2. Add `tool_use_id` column to `mcp_events`
3. Consider promoting `tool_input` to its own JSON column (parallel to `response_json`)

Requires a DB migration.

## Note

This issue is tracked here for visibility but the fix lives in the API repo, not the CLI.

items.title: fix: remove dead user_id field from CreateSessionRequest
items.body:
## Problem

The CLI populates `CreateSessionRequest.user_id` with the user's email/name, but the API completely ignores it — user identity is always derived from the OIDC bearer token.

This field is dead bytes on the wire and misleading in the proto definition (it implies the CLI controls user attribution, but it doesn't).

## Options

1. **Remove from proto** — delete the field, CLI stops sending it. Clean break.
2. **Keep as advisory** — document that it's informational only, API may ignore it. Useful for logging/debugging but not authoritative.

Recommend option 1 — the bearer token is the source of truth and having a dead field invites confusion.

items.title: feat: correlate PreToolUse and PostToolUse events via parent_event_id
items.body:
## Problem

PreToolUse and PostToolUse events for the same tool call are stored as independent rows with no explicit link between them. The only way to correlate them is by matching on `tool_use_id` within a session — which requires a query-time join and assumes `tool_use_id` is unique within a session.

The API supports a `parentEventId` field, but the CLI never sends it.

## Proposed solution

1. When the sidecar processes a PreToolUse event, the backend returns an `event_id` in the response
2. The sidecar stores a map of `tool_use_id → event_id`
3. When the corresponding PostToolUse arrives, the sidecar attaches the PreToolUse's `event_id` as `parent_event_id`
4. Add `parent_event_id` to the proto `ProcessHookEventRequest`

This gives the dashboard a direct parent→child link for every tool execution, enabling:
- Instant Pre→Post correlation without scanning
- Tool execution timeline visualization
- Duration calculation without query-time joins

## Dependency

Requires #31 (bidi streaming) or at minimum reading the `event_id` from the unary response, which the sidecar currently ignores.

items.title: feat: send CLI version, duration, and byte counts with events
items.body:
## Problem

Several fields that the API supports and stores are never populated by the CLI:

| Field | Current state | Impact |
|---|---|---|
| `clientVersion` | Never sent, always null | No way to know which CLI version generated an event — makes debugging and compatibility tracking impossible |
| `durationMs` | Hardcoded to `0` | No tool execution timing. For PostToolUse events, the time between Pre and Post is knowable but not calculated |
| `bytesIn` / `bytesOut` | Never computed | No payload size tracking despite having `tool_input` and `tool_response` data |

## Fix

### CLI version
- Add CLI version to `CreateSessionRequest.client_info` map (e.g. `{"name": "kontext-cli", "os": "darwin", "version": "0.1.0"}`)
- The version is already available via `ldflags` (`-X main.version=...`) from goreleaser

### Duration
- For PostToolUse events: compute elapsed time since the corresponding PreToolUse event (match by `tool_use_id`)
- The sidecar can maintain a map of `tool_use_id → start_time` from PreToolUse events
- Add `duration_ms` to the proto or compute it server-side by correlating Pre/Post events

### Byte counts
- Compute from `len(tool_input)` and `len(tool_response)` before sending
- Add `bytes_in` and `bytes_out` fields to the proto

items.title: fix: forward Claude Code session_id and permission_mode to backend
items.body:
## Problem

Two fields from Claude Code's hook stdin JSON are parsed but dropped before reaching the backend:

### 1. Claude Code's native `session_id`
- Parsed by the claude adapter in `DecodeHookInput`
- Stored in `agent.HookEvent.SessionID`
- **Dropped** in `main.go`'s `evaluateViaSidecar()` — the `EvaluateRequest` struct has no `SessionID` field
- The Kontext session ID is used instead, so Claude Code's own session identity is lost

### 2. `permission_mode`
- Parsed by the claude adapter's `hookInput` struct
- **Dropped** at the adapter layer — never transferred to `agent.HookEvent`
- This field indicates whether Claude Code is running in `default`, `plan`, or `bypassPermissions` mode — important security context

## Impact

- Cannot correlate Kontext events back to a specific Claude Code session (matters when multiple Claude instances share a Kontext session)
- No visibility into whether the agent was running with permissions bypassed — critical for audit/compliance

## Fix

1. Add `SessionID` and `PermissionMode` fields to `sidecar.EvaluateRequest`
2. Add corresponding fields to the proto `ProcessHookEventRequest`
3. Store both in the events table

items.title: fix: API ignores agent and cwd fields from ProcessHookEvent
items.body:
## Problem

The CLI populates `agent` and `cwd` in every `ProcessHookEventRequest`, but the API handler never reads them:

- **`agent`** — the agent type (e.g. "claude") is sent per event but discarded. Only stored once at session creation inside `client_info` JSON.
- **`cwd`** — the working directory per event is sent but completely ignored. This means if the agent changes directories during a session, that context is lost.

## Impact

- No way to filter/query events by agent type without joining to the session
- No per-event working directory in the audit trail — only the initial `cwd` from session creation
- Wasted bytes on the wire (minor)

## Fix

The API handler should read these fields and either:
1. Store them as first-class columns on `mcp_events` (preferred for queryability)
2. At minimum, include them in the `request_json` blob

items.title: feat: switch ProcessHookEvent from unary to bidi streaming for server-side policy decisions
items.body:
## Problem

The sidecar currently always returns `Allowed: true` synchronously to the hook handler, then fires off the `ProcessHookEvent` unary RPC asynchronously. The backend's `Decision` enum (`ALLOW`, `DENY`, `ASK`) is unused infrastructure — there's no path for the backend to actually deny a tool call.

This is because `ProcessHookEvent` is a unary RPC. The sidecar would have to block on the RPC round-trip for every tool call to get a decision, which adds latency to every agent action.

## Proposed solution

Switch `ProcessHookEvent` back to **bidirectional streaming**. The sidecar opens a persistent stream at session start and:

1. Sends each hook event as a message on the stream
2. Receives the policy decision (allow/deny/ask) back on the same stream
3. Returns the decision to the hook handler synchronously

This gives the backend a real enforcement path while keeping latency low (no connection setup per event — the stream is already open).

## Changes required

- **Proto** (`kontext-dev/proto`): Change `ProcessHookEvent` from `rpc ProcessHookEvent(ProcessHookEventRequest) returns (ProcessHookEventResponse)` to `rpc ProcessHookEvent(stream ProcessHookEventRequest) returns (stream ProcessHookEventResponse)`
- **CLI sidecar**: Open stream on session start, multiplex events onto it, wait for decisions before returning to hook handler
- **CLI backend client**: Replace `IngestEvent` unary call with stream send/receive
- **API handler**: Update ConnectRPC handler from unary to bidi streaming, evaluate policy per event, return decisions on the stream

## Design considerations

- Need a correlation ID per event so the sidecar can match responses to requests on the multiplexed stream
- Fallback behavior when stream disconnects: fail-open (allow) or fail-closed (deny)? Configurable?
- Latency budget: hook handlers need to respond in ~5-10ms. If the backend can't decide in time, should the sidecar fall back to a local decision?
- This pairs with future Cedar policy evaluation (#1) — local Cedar for fast decisions, server-side for complex/org-wide policy

## Related

- #1 — Agent credential isolation (policy enforcement is the other half of this problem)

items.title: design: first-run provider setup flow — how should the CLI populate .env.kontext?
items.body:
## Context

When a user runs `kontext start` for the first time in a project, there's no `.env.kontext` file. The CLI needs to figure out which providers to resolve credentials for. Today this file is manually created — the user should never have to do that.

## Possible flows

### Option A: Auto-populate from backend, no prompt

1. CLI fetches the org's configured providers from the backend
2. Writes `.env.kontext` with all of them (or a sensible default subset)
3. Resolves credentials — skips any that aren't connected yet
4. User commits the file, team shares it

**Pro:** Zero friction, instant start.
**Con:** May include providers the project doesn't need. File becomes org-level, not project-level.

### Option B: Auto-populate from backend, ask the user to confirm

1. CLI fetches available providers
2. Shows them: "These providers are available: GitHub, Linear, Slack. Which ones does this project need?"
3. User selects, CLI writes `.env.kontext`

**Pro:** Project-specific. Clean `.env.kontext`.
**Con:** Extra step on first run. Interactive prompt may not work in all environments (CI, etc.).

### Option C: Fetch connected providers only

1. CLI fetches only providers the current user has already connected in the dashboard
2. Writes `.env.kontext` with those
3. No prompt needed — if you connected it, you probably want it

**Pro:** Simple, no prompt. Only includes things the user actively set up.
**Con:** Different users may get different `.env.kontext` files. Doesn't capture project requirements.

### Option D: Start with a hardcoded default set

1. CLI writes `.env.kontext` with a default set (e.g. GitHub, Linear) without calling the backend
2. User edits if they need more or fewer

**Pro:** Simplest to implement. Works offline.
**Con:** Doesn't scale, not personalized.

### Option E: Hybrid — auto-populate, then let the user edit via `kontext providers`

1. First run: auto-populate from backend (option A or C) silently
2. Provide a `kontext providers` command to add/remove/list providers interactively later
3. `kontext start` always reads the file as-is

**Pro:** Fast first run + escape hatch for customization.
**Con:** Two commands to learn.

## Open questions

- Should `.env.kontext` be project-scoped (committed) or user-scoped (gitignored)?
- If committed, how do we handle different users having different providers connected?
- Should the CLI auto-create the file or require explicit `kontext init`?
- What about CI environments where there's no interactive prompt?
- How does the env var naming work? The backend knows the provider handle (`github`) but the env var name (`GITHUB_TOKEN`) is a project concern — who decides that mapping?

items.title: fix: CLI opens wrong URL for provider (re)authorization
items.body:
## Problem

When the token exchange returns `provider_reauthorization_required` or `provider_required`, the CLI tries to open `https://api.kontext.security/connect/{provider}` — that endpoint doesn't exist. The user sees a 404.

**Current code** (`internal/run/run.go:178`):
```go
connectURL := fmt.Sprintf("%s/connect/%s", auth.DefaultIssuerURL, entry.Provider)
```

This constructs `https://api.kontext.security/connect/github` which is the API, not the dashboard.

## How the token exchange flow works

### OAuth providers (e.g. GitHub, Slack)

1. User connects a provider in the dashboard (`app.kontext.security/providers/connect`) — this triggers an OAuth flow, and the backend stores a **refresh token** for the user
2. CLI runs `kontext start`, reads `.env.kontext`, and calls the backend's token exchange endpoint (RFC 8693) with the user's access token as `subject_token` and the provider as `resource`
3. Backend looks up the user's stored OAuth credential, uses the refresh token to mint a **short-lived access token**, and returns it
4. CLI injects the access token as an env var — the agent never sees the refresh token

**When it breaks:** The backend returns `provider_reauthorization_required` when:
- Provider config/scopes changed since the user last connected
- The stored refresh token is invalid or missing
- The credential is flagged for re-auth (`reconnectRequired`)

In this case, the user needs to redo the OAuth connect flow in the dashboard.

### API key providers (e.g. custom services)

1. User enters an API key in the dashboard (`app.kontext.security/providers/connect`) — the backend stores it encrypted (AES-256-GCM)
2. CLI calls token exchange with the provider as `resource`
3. Backend returns the decrypted API key directly
4. CLI injects it as an env var

**When it breaks:** The backend returns `provider_required` when no credential exists for that provider/user — the user needs to enter the key in the dashboard.

## Fix

The CLI should open the **dashboard** URL, not the API URL:

```go
connectURL := fmt.Sprintf("https://app.kontext.security/providers/connect")
```

This should be a configurable constant (not hardcoded to production) so it works in dev too.

### Considerations
- The dashboard connect page requires an authenticated browser session (BetterAuth cookie) — the user must be logged in to the web app
- The CLI's OIDC session is separate from the web app session — opening the dashboard URL may require the user to log in again if they don't have an active web session
- For API key providers, the connect page lets users paste keys manually — no OAuth redirect involved

items.title: feat: auto-refresh OIDC access token during long-lived sessions
items.body:
## Problem

The CLI authenticates via OIDC at `kontext start` and stores the access token for the session lifetime. The backend `bearerTransport` sends this token on every request (heartbeats, event ingestion, session end).

OIDC access tokens are short-lived (typically 1 hour with Hydra). For coding sessions that run longer than the token TTL, all authenticated requests start failing with `unauthenticated` — heartbeats, event ingestion, and session teardown all silently stop working.

```
2026/04/07 08:43:26 sidecar: heartbeat: unauthenticated: unauthenticated
2026/04/07 08:43:56 sidecar: heartbeat: unauthenticated: unauthenticated
...repeats every 30s for the rest of the session
```

## Desired behavior

The sidecar should transparently refresh the access token before or when it expires, without interrupting the session or requiring user interaction.

## Proposed approach

### 1. Persist the refresh token

The OIDC auth flow already returns a refresh token alongside the access token. Store it in the session (on disk or keyring) so it's available to the sidecar during the session.

### 2. Proactive refresh in the sidecar

The sidecar knows the token's `expires_at` time. Before expiry (e.g., when 80% of the TTL has elapsed), proactively use the `refresh_token` grant to obtain a new access token. Update the `bearerTransport` atomically so in-flight requests aren't affected.

### 3. Reactive refresh on 401

As a fallback, if any RPC returns `Unauthenticated`, attempt a refresh before retrying. This handles clock skew and edge cases where proactive refresh didn't fire in time.

### 4. Refresh failure → re-auth prompt

If the refresh token itself is expired or revoked, the sidecar can't recover silently. In this case, surface a clear message to the user (e.g., "Session expired, run `kontext login` to re-authenticate") rather than silently failing every 30 seconds.

## Implementation notes

- The `bearerTransport` in `internal/backend/backend.go` currently holds a static token string. It needs to become token-aware: hold a reference to a refreshable token source instead.
- The OIDC client registration must include `refresh_token` in its `grant_types`.
- The refresh token should be stored securely (system keyring or encrypted on disk), not as a plaintext env var.
- Consider making the `Client` struct hold a `TokenSource` interface that the sidecar can swap transparently, similar to `golang.org/x/oauth2.TokenSource`.

items.title: Wire full governance telemetry pipeline
items.body:
## Summary

Wire the complete telemetry pipeline so that `kontext start --agent claude` creates sessions visible in the Kontext dashboard, and every tool call / user prompt is logged as a governance event.

## Architecture

```
kontext start --agent claude
  ├── Backend client (REST bridge) → CreateSession
  ├── Sidecar (Unix socket) → heartbeat loop
  ├── Settings.json → Claude Code hooks → kontext hook
  ├── Hook events → sidecar → backend → mcp_events table
  └── On exit → EndSession → cleanup
```

## Implementation checklist

### Phase 0: Proto generation
- [ ] Create `buf.yaml` and `buf.gen.yaml`
- [ ] Generate Go code from `agent.proto` (ConnectRPC client + protobuf types)
- [ ] Add `connectrpc.com/connect` and `google.golang.org/protobuf` dependencies

### Phase 1: Backend client with REST bridge
- [ ] `internal/backend/config.go` — load credentials from env / config file
- [ ] `internal/backend/auth.go` — OAuth client_credentials token acquisition
- [ ] `internal/backend/client.go` — BackendService interface + REST bridge implementation

### Phase 2: Unix socket protocol
- [ ] `internal/sidecar/protocol.go` — length-prefixed JSON read/write

### Phase 3: Complete sidecar
- [ ] `internal/sidecar/sidecar.go` — handleConn, heartbeat, async event ingestion

### Phase 4: Hook command + settings generation
- [ ] `internal/run/hooks.go` — generate Claude Code settings.json
- [ ] `cmd/kontext/main.go` — wire hookCmd to call hook.Run() with sidecar callback

### Phase 5: Wire orchestrator
- [ ] `internal/run/run.go` — session create, sidecar start, settings gen, agent launch, session end

### Phase 6: Documentation
- [ ] Update README with telemetry strategy (governance vs observability)
- [ ] Document event types and tracing architecture

## Events captured

| Event | Source | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| `session.begin` | CLI lifecycle | Session shows in dashboard |
| `session.end` | CLI lifecycle | Session marked disconnected |
| `hook.pre_tool_call` | PreToolUse | Tool call authorization + telemetry |
| `hook.post_tool_call` | PostToolUse | Tool result for audit |
| `hook.user_prompt` | UserPromptSubmit | Prompt logging |

## Telemetry strategy

**Governance telemetry** (this issue): session lifecycle + tool call decisions + user prompts. Flows via sidecar → REST bridge → `mcp_events` table. Powers the Kontext dashboard.

**Developer observability** (future, separate): LLM generation details, token costs, reasoning traces. Langfuse or Dash0 via OTEL spans. Not in scope here.

## Server-side dependencies

Tracked in kontext-dev/kontext#405:
- `AgentService` gRPC endpoint (for native ConnectRPC, replacing REST bridge)
- CLI session-scoped token endpoint (eliminating manual client credentials)
- `agentSessionId` field on public mcp-events ingest endpoint

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `kontext start --agent claude` → session visible in Kontext dashboard
- [ ] Tool call in Claude Code → PreToolUse + PostToolUse events in traces
- [ ] User prompt → `hook.user_prompt` event in traces
- [ ] Exit Claude Code → session status = "disconnected"
- [ ] `kontext start --agent claude --local` → works without backend (events to stderr)

items.title: Agent credential isolation: tokens accessible via env vars bypass tool-level policy enforcement
items.body:
## Problem

When an agent session injects credentials as environment variables (e.g., `GH_TOKEN`, `AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID`) into a child process, the agent has **unrestricted access to the raw token values**. Tool-level policy enforcement (e.g., blocking specific tool calls) can be trivially bypassed because:

1. The agent can read env vars directly (`echo $GH_TOKEN`, `printenv`, `env`)
2. CLIs auto-consume credential env vars (`gh`, `git`, `aws` all read tokens from env automatically)
3. The agent can make arbitrary API calls via Bash (`curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" ...`)
4. Obfuscation is trivial (base64, Python one-liners, variable indirection, writing a script file then executing it)

**The fundamental tension:** env var injection is the simplest, most universal credential delivery mechanism — but it gives the agent process the same credential access as the user, making tool-level controls advisory rather than enforceable.

## Impact

- Cedar/OPA-style policy on tool calls can catch accidental or unsophisticated misuse, but a capable agent (or a prompt-injected agent) can bypass them trivially
- Short-lived tokens and narrow scoping reduce blast radius but don't prevent misuse during the session
- Audit trails detect misuse after the fact but don't prevent it

## Possible Solutions to Evaluate

### 1. Transparent credential proxy (strongest isolation)
Instead of injecting raw tokens, inject a proxy address:
```
HTTP_PROXY=http://localhost:<session-port>
HTTPS_PROXY=http://localhost:<session-port>
```
The sidecar intercepts outbound HTTP requests, injects auth headers for configured resources, and enforces policy at the **network level**. The agent never sees the raw token — it just makes unauthenticated requests that the proxy transparently upgrades.

**Pros:** Agent cannot exfiltrate tokens; policy enforcement at network level is robust
**Cons:** Complex to implement; breaks non-HTTP protocols; TLS interception requires CA trust; some CLIs don't respect proxy env vars

### 2. Credential-on-demand via sidecar (medium isolation)
Don't inject credentials as env vars at startup. Instead, the agent must request credentials through a local sidecar API (Unix socket), which:
- Returns short-lived, single-use tokens
- Logs every credential request
- Can deny requests based on policy
- Tokens have per-request TTLs (seconds, not session-length)

**Pros:** No long-lived tokens in env; every access is logged and policy-gated
**Cons:** Agent still receives the raw token in the response; requires CLI/tool integration

### 3. Process-level sandboxing (strongest but most restrictive)
Run the agent in a sandboxed environment (container, macOS sandbox profile, seccomp, network namespace) with:
- Outbound network restricted to an allowlist or routed through the credential proxy
- Filesystem access restricted to the project directory
- No access to credential env vars; credentials only flow through the proxy

**Pros:** Strongest isolation — even a fully compromised agent can't exfiltrate credentials
**Cons:** Severely limits agent capability; complex setup; platform-specific

### 4. Hybrid: policy enforcement + credential proxy for sensitive resources
- Low-sensitivity credentials (e.g., read-only GitHub token): inject via env vars, rely on Cedar policy + audit
- High-sensitivity credentials (e.g., write access, production DB): route through transparent proxy only

**Pros:** Pragmatic balance of security and usability
**Cons:** More complex architecture; requires classifying credential sensitivity

## Questions to Answer

- [ ] What is our threat model? Accidental misuse vs. prompt injection vs. malicious agent?
- [ ] Which solution provides the right tradeoff for our users?
- [ ] Can we implement transparent proxying without breaking existing CLI tool workflows?
- [ ] Should we support multiple isolation levels (env var injection for dev, proxy for prod)?
- [ ] How does this interact with MCP credential flows?

## References

- AWS Vault proxy mode: credential isolation via local HTTP proxy
- Docker credential helpers: credential-on-demand pattern
- macOS `sandbox-exec`: process-level network/filesystem restrictions
- Linux seccomp-bpf: syscall filtering for sandboxed processes
